title: Linking vegetation change with water availability in Peru
summary: I contributed satellite-data preparation and environmental time-series analysis to a NASA DEVELOP study of mesquite forest decline in Lambayeque, Peru. The team combined vegetation, rainfall, evapotranspiration and soil-moisture evidence to investigate changing conditions, while distinguishing observed associations from an established cause of forest mortality.
role: NASA DEVELOP team researcher · Data preparation and time-series analysis
context: Lambayeque, Peru · Mesquite forests and water resources

image.caption: Original NASA DEVELOP 2015 maps of precipitation, evapotranspiration, vegetation greenness and vegetation anomaly. Compare the study context and legends with the 2017 figure.

problem: Mesquite forest decline in Lambayeque required investigation across several environmental processes. A single vegetation index or rainfall series could not explain the whole system, so the team needed to compare water availability and vegetation condition across space and time.
contribution: I helped build the acquisition and preprocessing workflow that prepared NASA and other environmental observations for ArcGIS Pro. I also contributed to time-series analysis of NDVI, precipitation and soil moisture, bringing different datasets into a shared workflow for examining vegetation and water-resource patterns.

approach.title: Acquire and prepare the observations
approach.body: Used the shared NASA data-processing approach to automate acquisition and prepare satellite and environmental datasets for spatial analysis. The air-quality and water-resources studies used different products despite sharing processing methods.

approach.title: Compare vegetation and hydrologic conditions
approach.body: Examined NDVI and vegetation anomalies alongside precipitation, evapotranspiration and soil moisture. Each variable contributes a different part of the water–vegetation picture.

approach.title: Examine patterns through time
approach.body: Compared rainfall totals, evapotranspiration and soil-moisture depth series, including original 2001–2019 time-series figures. Considered how the timing and persistence of water availability coincided with vegetation conditions.

approach.title: Interpret evidence with the study limitations
approach.body: Compared the original 2015 and 2017 maps as visual evidence, while considering incomplete temporal coverage, coarse pixels and differences between satellite-derived patterns and local observations.

outcome: The team produced maps, time-series figures and a technical report documenting changing water and vegetation conditions. The poster reports declining precipitation over the study period, improved vegetation condition during wetter periods, and watershed-specific soil-moisture and evapotranspiration patterns. The analysis did not establish hydrology as the sole cause of mesquite mortality.
learning: This project demonstrates reuse of an observation-processing foundation across a different scientific problem. It adds the discipline of matching temporal coverage, spatial resolution and physical meaning before comparing datasets, and shows how a technical workflow can support environmental interpretation without turning correlation into a causal claim.
limitations: The analysis identifies environmental associations and does not independently determine the cause of mesquite mortality.
Incomplete temporal coverage and coarse-resolution mixed pixels constrain the comparisons; local partner observations did not always match NDVI patterns.
The 2015 and 2017 multi-panel maps have different layout and legend details. Visual comparison is not pixel-level change detection.
Modeled soil moisture is not a direct measure of mesquite root uptake, and rainfall alone does not describe water retained in the soil.

evidence.title: Original maps: 2015 and 2017
evidence.body: The two historical NASA DEVELOP figures show precipitation, evapotranspiration, NDVI and vegetation anomaly. They are retained as original research outputs rather than recreated results.

evidence.title: Evapotranspiration and soil moisture
evidence.body: Evapotranspiration combines surface evaporation and plant transpiration. Comparing it with moisture at several soil depths helps examine how water availability changes through time; neither variable independently establishes the cause of vegetation decline.

evidence.title: Precipitation baseline
evidence.body: The CHIRPS precipitation chart identifies wetter and drier periods for interpretation alongside the vegetation and soil-moisture series.
